newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: LME nickel rises on Inco strike, zinc to Singapore.
newsitem.headline: LME nickel rises on Inco strike, zinc to Singapore.

text.p: Nickel prices are seen rallying on the London Metal Exchange (LME) later on Tuesday after jumping as much as $200 in thin early Asian trade on overnight news of a strike at Inco Ltd's Sudbury smelter In Canada.

The union representing 4,670 workers at Sudbury announced the strike from just past midnight on Monday, local time, after its members voted to reject a previous tentative contract agreement with management.
"I think nickel is going to go up to US$7,300 (a tonne) on the LME," the general manager of a Japanese trading firm said. "They (Inco) have a very big share of the nickel market."
"Nickel should pop up back to around $7,220 on the LME, although I don't think it can go much higher than that," another trader said.
Three month LME nickel was quoted in Asian trade at around $7,170/220 a tonne at 0330 GMT, down from $7,215/20 at 0225 GMT, but still well above London's close on Monday at $7,025.
Nickel prices bounced back above $7,000 during afternoon trading on the LME on Monday, but remained easier after a substantial sell-off in the earlier session.

Losses were then induced by the now rejected tentative contract agreement at Inco's mining, smelting and refinery operations in Sudbury and the refinery in Port Colborne, Ontario reached over the weekend.
In the copper market, dealers were divided over the impact of a report from Shanghai on Tuesday that China's Central Reserve Bureau has no immediate plans to sell copper.

"They've (the Chinese) been selling lately. There's plenty of material which more than likely came from China," a dealer said, adding he did not believe Chinese merchants would pass on copper sales with prices hovering near $2,500 a tonne.
"There has been some copper offered by China as late as last week," a European metal company dealer said.
But a Japanese dealer said the report may make sense.
"Their domestic demand is increasing. Temporarily, they may stop copper exports," he said.
Copper prices are expected to regain a toehold above the $2,500 a tonne level later on Tuesday on the LME after the red metal closed on Monday at $2,485 a tonne.
Three month copper was quoted by the trade at 0400 GMT at around $2,492/97 a tonne.
"Copper should benefit from the coattails of nickel," one dealer said. "It might try to get back above $2,500. It seems to be consolidating and building a base around $2,500."
"I feel copper should firm up slightly," a Japanese dealer said. "We should see some consolidation at the $2,500 level."
In another development, rumours were swirling in the trade that up to 40,000 tonnes of zinc will be arriving in Singapore from China.

"There's a rumour that there's 40,000 tonnes of zinc coming here in the next few weeks. The rumour has it that the Chinese smelters have given about 40,000 to 50,000 tonnes of zinc to the merchants to sell," a dealer said.
Traders estimate that about 10,000 tonnes of zinc remain off-warrant in Singapore.
"That's going to drown the market," another dealer said.
But most traders believed the actual quantity of zinc on its way to the city-state would only amount to 5,000-6,000 tonnes.
The volume of zinc in the LME's Singapore warehouse reached 21,625 tonnes on Monday, up 10,375 tonnes from the level last week according to the exchange's latest stock figures.
